**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

Have never seen this attempted before.  At the very least, intermediate classes in declarative need to declare `__abstract__ = True`, assuming you don't want that class to be mapped, but that does not work here either.

**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

this seems to work however, can you try this:


```
        mapper(Person, person_table,
               polymorphic_on='kind', polymorphic_identity='person')

        class SpecialPerson(Person, Base):
            __abstract__ = True

        class Manager(SpecialPerson):
            __tablename__ = 'managers'
            id = Column(Integer, ForeignKey(Person.id), primary_key=True)
            __mapper_args__ = {
                'polymorphic_identity': 'manager'
            }

```

basically declarative doesn't know it needs to go down to Person in order to find "inherits" here.   will see what can be done.

**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

e.g., I dont even know how declarative finds "Person" in any case because it is below the base.

**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

right, so when it looks for the superclass of Manager, it finds SpecialPerson.  Then it asks, "is this non-mapped class declared as __abstract__?"  however, declarative only honors a flag like "__abstract__" if that class is part of the declarative hierarchy, if it's not, it doesn't want to assume anything.

so a new step would need to be added to test for this scenario explicitly.

**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

the issue is slightly sooner than that, the check for the `__abstract__` flag is showing the `Manager` as an abstract class itself and it isn't getting mapped, because it sees `SpecialPerson` as a mixin class.   which probably should not be the case if that class it itself classically mapped.

**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

Accommodate for classically mapped base classes in declarative

Fixed issue in previously untested use case, allowing a declarative mapped
class to inherit from a classically-mapped class outside of the declarative
base, including that it accommodates for unmapped intermediate classes. An
unmapped intermediate class may specify ``__abstract__``, which is now
interpreted correctly, or the intermediate class can remain unmarked, and
the classically mapped base class will be detected within the hierarchy
regardless. In order to anticipate existing scenarios which may be mixing
in classical mappings into existing declarative hierarchies, an error is
now raised if multiple mapped bases are detected for a given class.

Fixes: #4321
Change-Id: I8604ecfd170d2589d9d1b1c87ba303762071fc30


→ 4c931b2ec7e0

**Torsten Landschoff ([@bluehorn](https://github.com/bluehorn)) wrote:**

Thank you very much for fixing this. Unfortunately, something does not add up. I yet have to create a minimal example, but the symptoms are:

* I had in fact to add `__abstract__ = True` for the mixin classes of the classically mapped classes (even though your test case `test_intermediate_unmapped_class_on_classical` seems to cover that) or the bases were not detected. That would still have been good enough...
* After this I could not create relationships to the leaf class which appeared to not get mapped, this was fixed by adding `__abstract__ = False` for the concrete class.
* Finally, this lead to the error message: `InvalidRequestError: Class <class 'loco2.data.run.Run'> has multiple mapped bases: [<class 'loco2.data.entry.PoolEntry'>, <class 'loco2.data.entry.PoolEntry'>]`

I bet that a minimal example might not be so minimal, but the behaviour appears odd to me ;-)
Will open a new ticket for this as my original reproducer is obviously fixed.

**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

the thing you're trying to do is not something we've ever worked on so it's not surprising you are hitting issues.    you might be better off doing declarative from the bottom up, that is, it is likely easier to make a classical mapper inheriting from a declarative hierarchy rather than the other  way around.

**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

well you can't do multiple inheritance with classical mappings, and until now declarative was apparently silently failing, so now we've fixed that :).    I think whatever you have to do with the mixins, it's all good.      multiple inheritance could at least in theory work with single-table inheritance which is what you're doing, with joined inheritance it would be enormously difficult, but in either case, the level of redesign in the ORM would be enormous to accommodate this.  hence doing the multiple inheritance using non-mapped classes is the way to go.

issue.title: Missing guidance for migration from classical mappings to declarative mappings

labels.name: question
labels.description: issue where a "fix" on the SQLAlchemy side is unlikely, hence more of a usage question

issue.body:
Hello world,

we have a middle sized application that is using SQLAlchemy as the ORM. We started in 2011 with SQLAlchemy 0.6 when the declarative mapping style was still a new feature (and there was [Elixir](https://pypi.org/project/Elixir/) as an alternative).

Today we are still struggling with our mapping configuration. As our data model is mostly hierarchic (a version control system in a database) we have problems with circular dependencies.

With declarative this would be a non-issue given forward declarations. Also, IDE support would be much better (currently most column accesses are flagged as error given that the descriptors are added by calling the mapper on the existing class). Finally, to work around some issues we have classes that don't have any ORM related stuff in their home modules but a final `foo_bar_mapper.py` import attaches the mapper for multiple related classes.

This really sucks, therefore there have been multiple attempts to convert our code base to use the declarative extension. Some leaf classes have been converted but the core is still stuck.

We tried to go from the base classes downwards or from the leaf classes upward in conversion. But incremental conversion has been unsuccessful.

Therefore I would really like some guidance in the SQLAlchemy documentation about how to approach converting a non-simple code base from classical to declarative mapping. Are there any success stories to do this in an incremental way?

I'd like to help out here but so far all attempts were a dead end wrt. the hard parts.

Thanks and greetings,

Torsten

issue.title: Non-mapped mixin classes break ORM mapping

labels.name: declarative
labels.description: has to do with the declarative API, scanning classes and mixins for attributes to be mapped

issue.body:
Hi again,

it seems like I actually made things worse for us when reporting #4321. Our code actually mixes behaviour into our classes between the base class and the final concrete class. Nothing is mapped in those classes (truth to be told: one mixin class add relationships but from the ORM viewpoint we are still talking about single inheritance).

Here is a trivial example:

```
from sqlalchemy import *
from sqlalchemy.orm import *
from sqlalchemy.ext.declarative import *


Base = declarative_base()


class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = 'user'

    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    name = Column(String)
    surname = Column(String)


class SpecialUser(User):
    # Marker Interface only
    pass



class ConvenienceStuff(User):
    def fullname(self):
        return self.name + " " + self.surname


class Manager(SpecialUser, ConvenienceStuff, User):
    __tablename__ = 'manager'

    id = Column(Integer, ForeignKey('user.id'), primary_key=True)
    title = Column(String)
```

Running this with SQLAlchemy 1.3.4 I get this exception:

```
sqlalchemy.exc.InvalidRequestError: Class <class '__main__.Manager'> has multiple mapped bases: [<class '__main__.SpecialUser'>, <class '__main__.ConvenienceStuff'>, <class '__main__.User'>]
```

This seems incorrect to me given that there are no additions mapping-wise in `ConvenienceStuff` and `SpecialUser`.

Originally we didn't have the `User` base class BTW, but this is incorrent both because any IDE will claim that `fullname` does not have access to attributes `name` and `surname`. Also, the method resolution order can be messed up with this.

I tried adding `__abstract__ = True` to those mix in classes but this gives a rather weird exception that's not better in any way:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "decl_example.py", line 31, in <module>
    class Manager(SpecialUser, ConvenienceStuff, User):
  File "/opt/scalesdk/python27/lib/python2.7/site-packages/sqlalchemy/ext/declarative/api.py", line 75, in __init__
    _as_declarative(cls, classname, cls.__dict__)
  File "/opt/scalesdk/python27/lib/python2.7/site-packages/sqlalchemy/ext/declarative/base.py", line 131, in _as_declarative
    _MapperConfig.setup_mapping(cls, classname, dict_)
  File "/opt/scalesdk/python27/lib/python2.7/site-packages/sqlalchemy/ext/declarative/base.py", line 160, in setup_mapping
    cfg_cls(cls_, classname, dict_)
  File "/opt/scalesdk/python27/lib/python2.7/site-packages/sqlalchemy/ext/declarative/base.py", line 192, in __init__
    self._setup_inheritance()
  File "/opt/scalesdk/python27/lib/python2.7/site-packages/sqlalchemy/ext/declarative/base.py", line 574, in _setup_inheritance
    "Class %s has multiple mapped bases: %r" % (cls, inherits)
sqlalchemy.exc.InvalidRequestError: Class <class '__main__.Manager'> has multiple mapped bases: [<class '__main__.User'>, <class '__main__.User'>, <class '__main__.User'>]
```

Switching back to SQLAlchemy release 1.1.18 this works fine again (as the changes for #4321 were not merged into 1.1).

Greetings, Torsten
